newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe dismisses rumours of early election.
newsitem.headline: Juppe dismisses rumours of early election.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe dismissed on Thursday speculation that President Jacques Chirac might bring forward a general election scheduled for next March.
"I hear it said. It's in fashion. But the calendar is what it is," Juppe said in an interview to be published on Saturday in the weekly Le Figaro-Magazine.
Press reports have carried rumours that the president could dissolve parliament and call elections this spring in a bid to secure a conservative majority for the rest of his seven-year term.

The move would also avoid a collision between the election timetable and European Union plans to select countries early next year that qualify for a single European currency in 1999 under terms set by the Maastricht treaty on European union.

"You say that the campaign will be 'polluted' by Maastricht? Yes and no. Building a Europe with a currency, an army, an identity, isn't that one of the crucial questions for the future of France?" Juppe said.
Chirac has said repeatedly that a dissolution was not a matter of personal convenience and would only be justified to settle a political crisis.

In the interview, Juppe also vigorously attacked Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme-right National Front (FN) party and promised to wage a vocal fight against its values, which he called dangerous and "profoundly incompatible" with those of the French Republic.

"Some say we must not talk about the National Front. That's absurd. The National Front talks. Should we let it speak without answering? No, each time these ideas are put forward, I will rise up against them," Juppe said.

"How can we not fight against someone who has said the Holocaust and the (Nazi) ovens of the crematoriums were a 'detail' of history and who suggests that all of French society's problems can be solved by kicking out all the foreigners."
Juppe also said he was unconcerned by his poor showing in opinion polls, noting that other political leaders had faced bad poll results but later overcome them.
"I am guided by my convictions," he told the magazine.

A Louis Harris Institute poll for Valeurs Actuelles magazine said on Thursday Juppe's standing have declined this month after three months of gains with just 31 percent rating his performance good against 33 percent in March. The percentage with a bad impression climbed to 65 percent from 62.
A monthly IPSOS survey showed a similar result, with his approval rating falling to 29 from 31 percent while his disapproval rating was stable at 63 percent.
